newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Chemical weapons body relieved U.S. approves ban.
newsitem.headline: Chemical weapons body relieved U.S. approves ban.

text.p: The U.S. Senate's eleventh-hour ratification of an international treaty banning chemical weapons was an important step in ensuring its success, the Hague-based commission overseeing the accord said on Friday.
"I think relief is probably the best description of my feelings," said Ian Kenyon, executive secretary of the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW).
"We've been hoping for positive action from the U.S. Senate for a year and I have never lost faith that it was going to happen. But we got awfully close to the wire."
The Senate voted 74-26 on Thursday in favour of U.S. ratification of the Chemical Weapons Convention (CWC), which prohibits the development, production and use of chemical arms.

Only countries which ratify by Monday gain "State Party" status entitling them to vote at the first conference of the OPCW on May 6, which will shape the organisation tasked with enforcing the global ban.
"I think now that the U.S. is going to be a State Party, then some of the concerns that we had about how the first conference might pan out disappear," Kenyon said.
The United States and Russia are the world's largest possessors of chemical weapons, with declared stocks of 70,000 tonnes between them. Russia has not yet ratified the convention.
"We really wanted to have the two declared possessors, the two big states in world security, in there but half a loaf is better than no bread at all," he said.
Kenyon said though Russia would not now be in at the OPCW's inception, there was every indication that it would ratify the convention and join soon.

"The president has already sent the convention to the Duma, so the administration is aboard, and the Duma has indicated that it too sees the whole matter in a favourable light...and the only reason for a delay at this time is economic."
"They have concerns which have to be addressed, about how they find the money for destruction and things like that."
Russia's lower house of parliament on Friday postponed ratification of the treaty, saying it needed Western funds and more time to destroy its stockpile.
But it backed a draft law committing Russia in principle to destroying its weapons.
"The State Duma...has begun the process of ratifying the convention and intends to complete it if possible this autumn if the necessary conditions are met," it said in a statement.
The convention -- the first multilateral agreement to eliminate an entire category of weapons -- contains tough verification measures.
Signatories must destroy their chemical weapons within 10 years and provide detailed information about production and export of listed chemicals which could be used to make them.
They are barred from supplying listed chemicals to non-signatories and must open their chemical plants to the OPCW for both routine and short-notice inspections.
The OPCW has been training a multinational force of over 140 munitions specialists, analytical and industrial chemists and production logisticians as inspectors since January.

"The training is going very well," Kenyon said. "We have a small amount of inspection to do quickly, which is the operating destruction plants in the United States. Apart from that we have three or four months...to get started on the process."
Once that process is in place, states remaining outside the convention may face problems obtaining listed chemicals, even if they are needed by their industries for legitimate purposes.
Many of the so-called precursors used to make chemical weapons also have mundane uses in products like medicines, dyes and weedkillers.
